hook.description: Cold open at an upscale candlelit restaurant table. The weary, long-nosed male puppet says 'You're not listening to me' while a bold yellow text overlay 'YOU NEVER LISTEN TO ME' and an animated word-by-word caption ('LISTENING') stamp the accusation on screen, alongside a small 'Episode 34' label in the corner.
hook.why_it_works: The opening line doubles as the on-screen title, so the entire premise (a partner accusing the other of not listening) is legible within under 2 seconds with zero preamble - it drops viewers straight into a mid-argument moment they instantly recognize from real relationships.

setup.description: Cut to the woman across the table, who fires back defensively: 'I am literally looking at your face' (caption 'YOU'RE' visible). This establishes her side of the disagreement - she believes eye contact equals listening - and plants the misunderstanding the joke will exploit.

conflict.description: The man leans forward, raises a pointed finger, and escalates his rebuttal: 'You're waiting for me to finish so you can...' (captions 'AT' then 'FINISH'). His exaggerated brow and gesture visually build the tension of him explaining exactly why her claim of listening doesn't hold up.

punchline.description: The sentence lands on its final clause - '...say the thing you were already going to say' (caption 'WERE'). The joke is entirely verbal: a precise, relatable diagnosis that she isn't actually listening, just waiting for her turn to talk.

ending.description: A silent beat holds on the woman's face - eyebrows raised, mouth slightly open, visibly caught out with no comeback - before a hard cut to a black title card.
ending.cta_or_text_overlay: LOW BATTERY PEOPLE / CREATED BY NIN. (series title and creator credit end card; no explicit follow/like CTA)

story.narrative_notes: At under 10 seconds, hook and conflict are effectively fused: the opening line ('You're not listening to me') is both the cold-open hook and the first shot fired in the argument, so there is no separate scene-setting beat before the conflict begins. Setup is reduced to a single defensive line from the woman. The punchline is purely verbal (the final clause of one continuous sentence), not a visual sight gag or cutaway. The ending has two distinct parts - a brief silent 'caught out' reaction shot, then a separate black title/credit card ('LOW BATTERY PEOPLE, CREATED BY NIN.') that functions as series branding rather than a traditional CTA (no follow/like/comment prompt is present). The 'Episode 34' label in the hook signals this is one entry in a recurring character series, which substitutes for hook novelty since returning viewers already know the format.

dialogue.conversational_flow_notes: All three lines are delivered by a single transcribed speaker (SPEAKER_00) with no second voice on record, so the scene reads as one person confronting a silent/unresponsive counterpart rather than a back-and-forth exchange -- fitting a 'checked out, low battery' scene premise. There are zero cross-talk interruptions (each line starts cleanly after the previous one ends, with a measurable gap each time), and the three lines escalate in length and specificity: a blunt 5-word accusation, a 7-word rebuttal of evidence, then an 18-word explanation of the accusation's logic that lands as the punchline of the clip.
dialogue.speech_rhythm_notes: Line 1 ('You're not listening to me.', 5 words, 0.88s) opens after the clip's second-longest pause (0.503s of pre-roll silence from 0.0-0.503s). Line 2 (7 words, 1.62s) follows a short 0.243s gap (1.284-1.527s). Line 3 -- by far the longest line at 18 words and 4.25s -- follows the shortest inter-line gap of the three (0.259s, 3.053-3.312s), giving it almost no runway before the speaker launches into it. Within line 3 itself there is a brief 0.162s internal pause at 4.348-4.510s, which falls right at the clause break between '...finish so you can say' and 'the thing you were already going to say' -- a mid-sentence breath that sets up the punch clause rather than a between-line gap. The single longest pause in the clip (0.883s, 8.526-9.409s) occurs immediately after line 3 ends, leaving the accusation to sit in silence with no reply rather than being answered.

comedic_beats.description: Opening shot pairs the title card 'YOU NEVER LISTEN TO ME' and caption word 'LISTENING' directly over the man's droopy-eyed, heavy-lidded face before he speaks a single line.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The character rig's permanently half-closed, 'low battery' eyes already read as checked-out and disengaged, so stamping an accusation about not being listened to onto that exact face creates dramatic irony before any dialogue starts.

comedic_beats.description: He states 'You're not listening to me' in a flat, low-energy tone, mouth barely opening, no vocal escalation or raised volume.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The sagging eyebrows and downturned mouth deliver a serious relational accusation with zero visible urgency, so the total mismatch between the emotional weight of the line and the flat, sleepy delivery is the joke itself.

comedic_beats.description: After a 0.24s beat of silence, he snaps to 'I am literally looking at your face,' punctuating it with a raised, pointed finger (seen in the scene-2 keyframe), while his eyes remain half-lidded and drowsy.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The emphatic word 'literally' plus the jabbing finger gesture promise focused attention, but the character's perpetually sleepy eye design visually contradicts the claim in real time, an irony that's baked into the show's whole visual identity, not just this line reading.

comedic_beats.description: The sentence builds through 'You're waiting for me to finish' and then hits a 0.162s micro-pause (4.348-4.51s) right after the word 'finish' before continuing into the punchline clause.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: That hair's-width pause mimics the exact behavior being described in the line, a beat where he could yield the floor but doesn't, letting the audience feel the 'waiting to jump in' dynamic land in real time rather than just hearing it described.

comedic_beats.description: The line resolves into '...so you can say the thing you were already going to say,' naming the precise, granular habit of pretend-listening while queueing your own response, delivered as one unbroken sentence with no reaction shot from the woman, whose back stays turned to camera the whole scene.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: It names a specific micro-behavior most viewers instantly recognize from their own conversations rather than a generic 'you don't listen' complaint, and withholding any cutaway to her face makes the accusation feel aimed straight at the viewer.

comedic_beats.description: The longest pause in the piece (0.88s, roughly triple the earlier gaps) sits over his open, deflated expression before a hard cut to black and the 'LOW BATTERY PEOPLE / Created by Nin.' title card, with no reply from the woman.
comedic_beats.why_it_lands: The scene cuts to the show's own logo instead of giving the dinner partner a comeback, leaving the accusation completely unanswered, which mirrors the exact one-sided non-conversation he just complained about.

comedy.overall_comedic_style_notes: The series' signature device is a visual/verbal irony built into the puppet design itself: every character has permanently heavy-lidded, sleepy 'low battery' eyes, so any emotionally charged or urgent line reads as flat and deadpan by default, letting a single unbroken monologue (here, one continuous rant across three short lines and roughly 9 seconds) carry both the joke and the relatable sting without needing punchline delivery or a reaction shot. The scene partner is kept faceless (shot from behind) for the entire runtime, turning what looks like a two-hander into a direct-address confession, and the piece resolves not with a joke but with unresolved silence (the longest pause of the clip) before cutting straight to the show's branding, favoring a relatable gut-punch about being unheard over a comedic release.

shots.composition_notes: Static medium two-shot at the dinner table: the man (huge stylized nose, black suit) is left-of-center facing camera, the woman is a soft-focus silhouette in the near-right foreground with her back to camera, creating a shallow-depth-of-field frame within a frame. 'Episode 34' watermark pinned top-left; oversized bold yellow caption 'YOU NEVER LISTEN TO ME' is centered over the middle third of the frame, overlapping the subject's torso rather than avoiding it. A lit candle sits dead-center on the table as a foreground anchor.

Extremely brief (0.1s) reverse-angle cutaway: man's head and shoulders seen from behind on the left edge, woman now frontal and in focus on the right, caption 'YOU'RE' bottom-center. Functions as a whip-fast reaction beat rather than a sustained shot -- man's back-of-head is cropped tight against the left frame edge.

Hard cut to an extreme close-up of the man's face, dead-center and frontal, nose filling the vertical middle of frame. Raised index finger enters from lower-left as a punctuation gesture on 'literally' and 'face.' Background restaurant lights are reduced to soft bokeh circles, isolating the face against negative space -- no headroom cushion, chin and hairline both near frame edges.

Cut back out to a medium head-and-shoulders shot, man centered against his booth's black chair back, delivering 'for' / 'so' with a flat, unimpressed expression. Same restaurant bokeh background and candle-in-frame staging as the opening shot, but text overlay is gone -- captions now sit small and low, out of the way of the face.

Camera punches in on the word 'thing,' pushing from the medium shot to a perfectly symmetrical frontal extreme close-up -- nose runs exact center vertical axis, eyes level left-right, mouth barely visible at the bottom edge. The symmetry itself reads as the joke's visual beat, framing the face like a deadpan mugshot.

Holds the punched-in extreme close-up from the previous beat -- still dead-center symmetrical framing, caption 'were' low in frame. No further movement; the static hold lets the exaggerated features (droopy eyes, huge nose) sit as the entire visual joke.

Slight angle change to a three-quarter close-up, man's face tilted and eyes cast down/sideways in a resigned, sad expression -- less strictly symmetrical than the prior shot, giving a softer, more vulnerable read for the line's resolution. Near the end of this shot the outro title card ('LOW BATTERY PEOPLE / CREATED BY NIN.') begins fading in as a text overlay directly on top of this live face, blending the last story beat into the outro.

Pure black background outro/branding card: centered gold serif title 'LOW BATTERY PEOPLE' with smaller white 'CREATED BY NIN.' beneath it, and a yellow 'NEW EPISODE DAILY' ribbon graphic animating in below. No camera or subject present -- purely a static graphic end card.

camera.framing_patterns_notes: The video alternates between two framing extremes with almost nothing in between: a medium/wide establishing composition only at the very start (with the bold caption text overlapping the subject rather than sitting in clear space), and then a string of tight-to-extreme close-ups for every subsequent beat, culminating in a hard zoom-in punch on the word 'thing' that lands on a perfectly symmetrical, dead-center face -- the visual punchline mirrors the verbal one. The over-the-shoulder reverse angle is used exactly once, as a near-subliminal 0.1s reaction cutaway rather than a sustained shot. Low-set, small caption text is used consistently under the chin/collar so it never competes with the exaggerated facial features, except in the opening shot where oversized title-card-style text is deliberately laid over the frame. The outro title card is foreshadowed by dissolving text directly onto the final live-action close-up before cutting to a clean black card, rather than a hard cut to the branding screen.

animation.technique: Reads as 3D CGI built to evoke a stop-motion/felted-puppet look (fuzzy fabric-like skin and coat texture, matte clay-style highlights, oversized conical nose, simple flat-dot pupils) rather than literal frame-by-frame practical stop-motion. Evidence against true stop-motion: perfectly smooth cinematic rack-focus/bokeh on background lights, no visible fingerprints or armature wobble, and no duplicate/held poses across the sampled periodic frames. Uncertain whether it is fully rendered 3D or a hybrid pipeline, but the motion behavior across keyframes points to rigged/interpolated animation with a deliberately handmade surface shader.
animation.facial_animation_notes: Eyebrows are the primary expressive channel: heavy dark brows swing between a lowered, skeptical furrow (periodic-0, 1, 4, 5, 6, wide shots) and a sharply raised, arched shock pose with fully round eyes (periodic-3, 7, 8, close-ups). Mouth shapes are simple open/closed poses timed to on-screen caption words ("TO", "FOR", "SO", "THING") with visible teeth/tongue detail on wide-open frames; between lines the mouth resets to a static downturned neutral shape rather than showing co-articulation or lip-sync nuance.
animation.eye_and_blink_notes: No blinks appear in any of the 10 sampled periodic frames - eyes stay open throughout, with pupils as simple flat black dots. The eyes carry most of the emotional swing, moving from droopy/hooded half-closed lids in wide shots to fully round, white-dominant 'shocked' eyes in close-up reaction frames; gaze direction shifts (side-eye toward the listener vs. a more direct stare) but no independent eye-dart or saccade animation is visible between frames.
animation.head_movement_notes: In wide two-shots (periodic-0, 1, 4, 5, 6) the male character's head holds a near-static three-quarter profile with only tiny tilts on emphasized words; the sense of movement in those beats comes largely from eyebrow/eye changes, not head rotation. In close-ups (periodic-2, 3, 7, 8) the head appears tilted back slightly as if mid-rant, but this reads partly as a reframe/push-in rather than pure character head motion. The woman across the table (seen only from behind, out of focus) shows no visible head movement across any sampled frame - she functions as a static listening prop.
animation.gesture_notes: A single raised index-finger gesture appears in periodic-2 and periodic-3 (hand lifted near the face, finger pointed up, ring visible on the finger) held through the word "literally" as a classic exasperated-point beat; the hand is out of frame by the following close-up. In wide shots (periodic-0, 1, 5, 6) both characters' hands rest passively at the table edge with no other gesticulation visible.
animation.idle_motion_notes: Background diners visible as soft bokeh silhouettes at other tables show no discernible independent motion across the sampled frames - they read as static set dressing rather than looping idle animation. The string/fairy lights in the background hold consistent bokeh circle size and brightness frame to frame (no flicker or twinkle animation), and the foreground candle shows no visible flame-flicker variation between frames.
animation.frame_rate_feel: Metadata reports 30fps. Periodic frames sampled roughly one second apart show continuous, non-repeating pose changes with no evidence of duplicated/held frames within that sampling window, and there is no visible motion blur on any frame - edges stay crisp even on the moving hand gesture. Combined, this feels like clean, smooth-at-source or well-interpolated animation rather than a deliberate low-fps stop-motion stutter, despite the felted stop-motion-style surface texture suggesting that look was the intended reference.
animation.overall_animation_style_notes: The short leans on a 'prestige stop-motion' aesthetic - fuzzy felt-like skin/fabric shading, an oversized nose, sleepy hooded eyes, and bold eyebrows in an Aardman/Laika-adjacent character design - paired with polished cinematography (shallow depth of field, warm restaurant bokeh, smooth pushes between a wide 2-shot and tight reaction close-ups) that behaves more like contemporary CG than handmade animation. Comedic delivery is carried almost entirely by eyebrow/eye extremes and one punctuating finger-point gesture rather than full-body or background performance, keeping the dialogue-driven 'episode' format visually simple and fast to read.

cuts.reason: Snaps to a near-subliminal (0.1s) reaction cutaway of the woman during the pause right after 'You're not listening to me,' letting her blank stare hang for a beat before he keeps talking.
Cuts back to the man's tight close-up as he resumes with 'I am literally looking at your face,' timed to the restart of dialogue after the micro-pause.
Pulls back to a wider two-shot at the table right as he launches into the longest, most escalating line ('You're waiting for me to finish...'), resetting the frame for the accusation's build-up.
Punches straight in on his face without a real camera move, landing right on the word 'were' -- the twist word that reveals he's already rehearsing his comeback -- for punchline emphasis.
Cuts immediately to the woman's guilty, wide-eyed reaction shot the instant the accusation lands, letting her silent expression deliver the joke instead of a line.
Hard cut to the black end-card/logo screen ('LOW BATTERY PEOPLE') once the reaction has had a moment to breathe, closing out the sketch.

editing.pacing_notes: The cut opens with a 1.4s title-card/hook shot, then snaps into a nearly subliminal 0.1s reaction cutaway during the first pause -- an early comedic jab. It settles into a 1.7s close-up, then expands to the longest shot of the video (2.6s) to carry the escalating, multi-clause accusation line. Right on the word 'were' it punches into a much tighter, shorter (~1s) close-up for emphasis on the reveal. It then holds a bit longer (~1.4s) on the woman's silent reaction shot to let the punchline land, before a final ~1.2s hard cut to the end card. Overall the rhythm is not a steady acceleration but a wind-up-and-release pattern: shots lengthen through the setup and long accusation line, snap short right on the punchline word, then lengthen again for the reaction and outro.
